question: You receive an email from 'security@bankofamer1ca-alerts.net' saying your account has been locked. What should you do FIRST?
options: Click the link in the email to verify your identity
Reply to the email asking for more information
Call the number on the back of your bank card to verify
Forward the email to your friends to warn them
explanation: Always call your bank using the phone number on the back of your debit or credit card — never use contact information provided in a suspicious email. The email domain 'bankofamer1ca-alerts.net' uses a '1' instead of 'i' and is not the real Bank of America domain.

question: Which of the following is the BIGGEST red flag in a suspicious email?
options: The email includes the company's logo
The sender's email domain doesn't match the real company
The email was sent during business hours
The email includes a customer service phone number
explanation: The sender's domain is the most reliable indicator. Scammers can easily copy logos, write during business hours, and include fake phone numbers — but they cannot send from a real company's domain. Always check the full email address, not just the display name.

question: You receive a text saying: 'IRS: You have a pending refund of $1,847. Claim now.' What makes this definitely a scam?
options: The refund amount seems too high
The IRS never contacts people by text message
It was sent on a weekend
The text doesn't include your name
explanation: The IRS NEVER initiates contact via text message, email, or social media. All legitimate IRS communications begin with a letter sent through the U.S. Postal Service. Any text claiming to be from the IRS is automatically a scam, regardless of the amount or other details.

question: Your 'grandchild' texts asking for $5,000 in bail money via gift cards and begging you not to tell their parents. What should you do?
options: Send the gift cards quickly since they're in trouble
Ask them security questions only your real grandchild would know
Hang up and call your grandchild directly at their known phone number
Go to the police station to pay the bail in person
explanation: Always hang up and contact your grandchild directly using a phone number you already have saved. The 'grandparent scam' works by creating panic so you act before thinking. Key facts: legitimate bail is NEVER paid with gift cards, and the request for secrecy is designed to prevent you from verifying the story.

question: A pop-up appears in your browser saying 'Microsoft has detected 3 viruses on your computer! Call 1-800-555-0199.' What should you do?
options: Call the number immediately to get help
Write down the error code and search for it online
Close the browser completely — it's a scam
Run your antivirus software by clicking the pop-up button
explanation: Close the browser immediately. Microsoft NEVER displays phone numbers in virus warnings, and real antivirus alerts don't appear as browser pop-ups. If the browser won't close, use Ctrl+Alt+Delete (Windows) or Force Quit (Mac) to close it. These pop-ups want you to call so scammers can get remote access to your computer.

question: A website pop-up says it has scanned your computer and found 13 viruses. This is:
options: Probably real if it shows specific virus names
Real only if you have antivirus software installed
Always fake — websites cannot scan your computer
Real if it asks you to pay for removal
explanation: A website CANNOT scan your computer for viruses — this is technically impossible due to browser security restrictions. Any pop-up claiming to have scanned your computer and found threats is 100% fake, every single time, no exceptions. Only antivirus software you have installed on your computer can perform real scans.

question: Someone on Facebook Marketplace wants to buy your item for $500 but sends you a check for $2,000, saying the extra is for 'shipping.' What is happening?
options: They made an honest mistake with the check amount
It's an overpayment scam — the check is fake
They want to make sure shipping is covered
It's a sign they're a generous buyer
explanation: This is the classic 'overpayment scam.' The check is counterfeit. Your bank may initially make the funds available, but when the check bounces days later, the bank will take back the full amount. Meanwhile, any money you wired for 'shipping' is gone forever. Legitimate buyers NEVER overpay and ask for change back.

question: What is the SAFEST way to pay for an item on a local marketplace like Facebook Marketplace or Craigslist?
options: Wire transfer — it's fast and reliable
Gift cards — they're easy to use
Cash, in person, at a public location
Zelle or Venmo sent before seeing the item
explanation: Cash in person at a public place (like a police station lobby) is the safest for local marketplace transactions. Wire transfers and gift cards are untraceable and non-refundable — scammers' preferred payment methods. Zelle and Venmo offer no buyer protection for goods. Never send money before seeing and inspecting the item in person.

question: An email from 'geeksquad-renewal@outlook.com' says you've been charged $349.99 for auto-renewal. The email wants you to call a phone number to cancel. Why is the email address suspicious?
options: Geek Squad doesn't offer renewals
The price is too high for Geek Squad
Geek Squad / Best Buy would use @bestbuy.com, not @outlook.com
Outlook.com emails are always scams
explanation: Legitimate businesses send emails from their own domain (like @bestbuy.com), not from free email services like Outlook.com, Gmail.com, or Yahoo.com. A free email domain is one of the easiest red flags to spot. The scammers want you to call their fake number where they'll try to get remote access to your computer.

question: You receive a text about an unpaid toll of $4.15 with a link to pay. How should you handle this?
options: Pay the small amount to avoid the penalty — it's only $4.15
Click the link to check if you really owe money
Ignore the text and check your toll account directly through the official website or app
Reply STOP to unsubscribe from the messages
explanation: Never click links in unexpected texts. The small $4.15 amount is designed to seem harmless, but the link captures your credit card and personal information. If you use toll roads, check your account directly through the official toll agency's website or app. Toll agencies send bills through postal mail, not text messages.

question: You see a pop-up saying your Chrome browser needs an urgent security update and you should download it now. What should you know?
options: You should always update when prompted for security
Chrome updates automatically — pop-up update prompts are fake and may install malware
You need to verify the update version number before downloading
Only download the update if it shows the Google logo
explanation: Chrome and most modern browsers update automatically in the background. A pop-up asking you to download an update is actually trying to trick you into downloading malware. To manually check for Chrome updates, go to Menu (three dots) > Help > About Google Chrome. Never download software from a pop-up.

question: A Facebook Marketplace seller is offering purebred puppies for $200 (normally $1,500) and wants payment via Zelle before shipping the puppy to you. What are the warning signs?
options: The price is reasonable for online puppy sales
Price far below market value, can't meet in person, payment via Zelle with no buyer protection, and shipping live animals
Zelle is a safe payment method for online purchases
Shipping puppies is a normal practice for breeders
explanation: This has every hallmark of a pet scam: a price that's too good to be true, inability to meet in person, payment via a method with no buyer protection (Zelle), and offering to 'ship' an animal. After payment, they'll request more fees for 'shipping insurance' or a 'temperature-controlled crate.' The puppy doesn't exist. Always meet pets in person before any payment.

question: An email that looks like it's from Amazon says your account is locked and asks you to "click here to verify." What's the safest thing to do?
options: Open the Amazon app or type amazon.com yourself to check your account
Click the link, but be careful what you type
Reply and ask if the email is real
Call the phone number in the email
explanation: Go to the company yourself, using the app or a web address you type. Links, phone numbers, and replies in a suspicious email all lead back to the scammer.

question: Which sender address is MOST likely to be a scam?
options: alerts@chase.com
support@paypa1-security.com
service@paypal.com
no-reply@amazon.com
explanation: "paypa1" uses the number 1 instead of the letter l, and adds extra words. Scammers make addresses that look right at a quick glance.

question: You clicked a link in a phishing email and typed in your email password. What should you do right away?
options: Nothing, since you can't undo it
Delete the email so the scammer can't see it
Change that password, and any other account using the same password
Wait to see if anything strange happens
explanation: Change the password right away, starting with your email account, and anywhere else you used the same password. If you shared bank details, call your bank too.

question: You get a text: "Did you make a $750 purchase at Best Buy? Reply YES or NO." What should you do?
options: Reply NO so the bank blocks it
Reply YES so they leave you alone
Call the number that texted you
Don't reply. Check your account in your bank's app, or call the number on your card
explanation: Any reply tells the scammer your number works, and often leads to a call from a fake "fraud department." Check with your bank yourself.

question: How can you report a scam text to your phone company?
options: Forward it to 7726 (SPAM)
Reply STOP
Call 911
Text it to a friend
explanation: Forwarding a scam text to 7726 reports it to most U.S. phone companies so they can block it. Then delete it and block the number.

question: A stranger texts "Hi, is this Linda? Are we still on for lunch?" You're not Linda. A friendly chat starts and later turns to investing. What's happening?
options: A lucky new friendship
A common scam that starts with a fake wrong-number text
A marketing survey
A real mistake you should keep chatting about
explanation: "Wrong number" texts are often how romance and investment scams start. The best response is no response.

question: A warning fills your screen with a loud alarm and won't close. What should you do?
options: Call the number to get help
Click the warning to see what it says
Close the browser, or restart the computer if it won't close
Pay for the antivirus it offers
explanation: It's just a web page designed to scare you. Closing the browser or restarting ends it. Your computer is almost always fine.

question: A "technician" on the phone asks you to install a program so he can fix your computer remotely. What should you do?
options: Install it, since he's trying to help
Install it, but watch what he does
Ask him to email you the program instead
Hang up. Never let someone who contacted you connect to your computer
explanation: Remote access gives scammers full control of your computer and possibly your bank accounts. Only let trusted people you contacted yourself, like a family member or a shop you chose, work on your computer.

question: You let a fake tech-support caller into your computer. What should you do FIRST?
options: Turn off the computer or disconnect it from the internet
Call them back to ask for a refund
Keep using the computer as normal
Pay what they ask so they leave you alone
explanation: Cut off their access first. Then have a trusted person check the computer, change your passwords from a different device, and call your bank.

question: A buyer asks you to read them a 6-digit code sent to your phone "to prove you're a real seller." What should you do?
options: Read it, since it shows you're honest
Never share it. It lets them take over your account
Share only the first 3 digits
Email it instead of reading it aloud
explanation: That code is meant only for you. Scammers use it to set up accounts in your name or break into yours. No real buyer needs it.

question: When shopping on a website you don't know, which way of paying gives you the MOST protection?
options: Gift card
Wire transfer
Credit card
Zelle to the seller
explanation: Credit cards let you dispute charges if the item never arrives. Gift cards, wire transfers, and payment apps sent to strangers are very hard to get back.

question: A seller has concert tickets for half price but can't meet and wants payment through Venmo first. This is:
options: A great deal, so pay quickly
Normal for tickets
Safe if they send a photo of the tickets
A warning sign. Don't pay someone you can't meet for an item you can't see
explanation: Too-good prices plus "pay first, can't meet" is a classic marketplace scam. Photos of tickets are easy to fake or sell to many people.

question: A caller sounds exactly like your grandson. He says he's in jail and needs bail money, and begs you not to tell his parents. What should you do?
options: Hang up and call your grandson or his parents on numbers you know
Send the money, since it's his voice
Ask the caller to prove it by telling you his birthday
Pay half now and half later
explanation: Scammers can now copy a voice with AI, and birthdays are often on social media. Calling family back on known numbers, or using a family code word, is the reliable check.

question: Your caller ID shows your bank's real name and number. Can you trust it?
options: Yes, caller ID can't be faked
No, scammers can make any name or number appear
Only if it's a local number
Only if they know your name
explanation: This is called "spoofing." Scammers can fake caller ID easily. Hang up and call the number on the back of your card.

question: A caller from your bank's "fraud team" asks you to move your savings to a "safe account" to protect it. This is:
options: A smart precaution
Normal during fraud investigations
Always a scam. Real banks never ask you to move money to protect it
Fine if they give you a case number
explanation: Real banks protect your money where it is. A "safe account" belongs to the scammer.

question: What's a family code word for?
options: Logging in to your bank
Your email password
Getting discounts
A secret word real family members can say to prove an emergency call is really them
explanation: Agree on a word ahead of time. If a "grandchild" or "relative" calls in a panic and can't say it, hang up and call them back.

question: Which payment request should ALWAYS make you hang up?
options: "Pay with gift cards and read me the numbers"
"Pay with a check by mail"
"Pay through our official website"
"Mail us your bill"
explanation: No real business or government agency takes payment in gift cards. Asking for gift card numbers means it's a scam.

question: You get a robocall offering a "free" back brace covered by Medicare if you confirm your Medicare number. What should you do?
options: Give the number, since it's free
Hang up. Never give your Medicare number to someone who called you
Ask them to mail the brace first
Give only your date of birth
explanation: Scammers use your Medicare number to bill for equipment you never receive. Treat it like a credit card number.

question: Someone says they're from the IRS and that police will arrest you today unless you pay with gift cards. What's true?
options: You should pay quickly to avoid arrest
The IRS only takes gift cards for small amounts
The IRS doesn't threaten arrest or ask for gift cards, so it's a scam
You should ask for their badge number, then pay
explanation: The IRS normally contacts you by mail first and never demands gift cards, wire transfers, or crypto. Hang up and call 1-800-829-1040 if you're worried.

question: A caller says your Social Security number has been "suspended." What's true?
options: You need to reactivate it right away
Only Medicare can fix it
You should give them your number to check
Social Security numbers can't be suspended, so it's a scam
explanation: Social Security numbers are never suspended. This is a scare tactic to get your number and bank details.

question: What's the real phone number for Social Security?
options: The number in the text or voicemail you got
Any number with "SSA" on caller ID
There is no phone number
explanation: Social Security's real number is 1-800-772-1213. Always call agencies on official numbers, which you can find on their .gov websites, never the number a caller gives you.

question: How do you know a government website is real?
options: It has an official-looking eagle logo
Its address ends in .gov
It has a .org or .com address with "gov" in it
It loads quickly
explanation: Real U.S. government websites end in .gov, like irs.gov and ssa.gov. Logos are easy to copy; the web address is what matters.

question: An email says you've won a $9,000 government grant but must pay a $250 processing fee. What should you do?
options: Pay the fee to get the grant
Reply with your bank details
Ignore and delete it. The government doesn't charge fees to give you money
Pay with a gift card to be safe
explanation: Paying a fee to receive free money is always a scam. The government doesn't hand out surprise grants by email.

question: Medicare calls to say they're sending you a new card and need your Medicare number and bank account. What's true?
options: You should give it so you get the new card
Only give the bank account
Give it if they're polite
Medicare won't call you uninvited to ask for this, so it's a scam
explanation: Medicare won't call you out of the blue for your Medicare number or bank account. Call 1-800-MEDICARE if you have questions.

question: Someone you met online a few weeks ago says they love you, but they can never video chat. Now they need money for a medical emergency. What should you do?
options: Don't send money. These are classic signs of a romance scam
Send a small amount to help
Send gift cards instead of cash
Ask them to pay you back first
explanation: Quick love, no video calls, and a money emergency are the classic pattern. Never send money to someone you've only met online.

question: Why do romance scammers ask you to move from the dating site to WhatsApp or texting?
options: Because texting is easier
To get away from the dating site's safety checks
Because they're shy
To save you money
explanation: Dating sites watch for and remove scam profiles. Moving you off the site lets scammers keep going without being caught.

question: Your online partner says they're a deployed soldier who needs you to pay a "leave fee" so they can come home. What's true?
options: Military leave fees are normal
You should pay through their agent
The U.S. military doesn't charge leave fees, so it's a scam
It's fine if they send a photo in uniform
explanation: Scammers often pose as soldiers using stolen photos. The military doesn't charge fees for leave or travel.

question: What's a good way to check whether an online sweetheart's photos are real?
options: Ask them for more photos
Trust them because the photos look natural
Ask their friends
Do a reverse image search to see if the photos appear under other names
explanation: A reverse image search, such as Google Images or TinEye, often shows that scam photos were stolen from someone else. A family member can help you do it.

question: An online sweetheart says they mailed you a gift, and now a "customs company" wants a fee to release it. What should you do?
options: Don't pay. There is no package; it's part of the scam
Pay so you get the gift
Pay half the fee
Ask the customs company for a discount
explanation: Fake customs and delivery fees are a common next step in romance scams. Each fee leads to another.

question: Your online partner asks you to keep your relationship secret from your family. This is:
options: Romantic
A warning sign. Scammers want to stop family from warning you
Normal for new relationships
A sign they're shy
explanation: Secrecy keeps the people who love you from spotting the scam. Talking to someone you trust is one of the best protections.

question: Which of these is the BIGGEST warning sign of an investment scam?
options: The company has a website
They mention the stock market
"Guaranteed" high returns with no risk
They send you paperwork
explanation: All real investments carry risk. Anyone guaranteeing high returns is lying.

question: A trading app shows you've made $40,000, but says you must pay a 20% "tax" before you can withdraw. What's going on?
options: Normal investment taxes
A small fee worth paying
A bank error
A scam. The balance is fake and the money you deposited is gone
explanation: Real platforms take fees from your balance. Demanding more money before you can withdraw is how fake trading apps take even more.

question: Someone on the phone tells you to withdraw cash and put it into a Bitcoin ATM to keep it safe. What should you do?
options: Hang up. No real bank or agency will ever tell you to use a Bitcoin ATM
Do it quickly before hackers get it
Ask the bank teller to help you use the ATM
Only put in half
explanation: Being told to use a Bitcoin ATM means it's a scam, every time. Money sent this way is almost impossible to recover.

question: Where can you check whether a person or company is allowed to sell investments?
options: Their own website
brokercheck.finra.org and investor.gov
Their social media reviews
A WhatsApp group
explanation: FINRA BrokerCheck and the SEC's investor.gov let you look up licensed brokers and advisers, and see any past problems, for free.

question: After losing money to a scam, you're contacted by a company that promises to recover it for an upfront fee. This is:
options: A lucky break
How law enforcement usually works
Very likely a second scam, called a recovery scam
Worth it if the fee is small
explanation: Recovery scammers target people who've already lost money. Report losses for free at ic3.gov and reportfraud.ftc.gov instead.

question: A friendly stranger in a WhatsApp group shares screenshots of huge profits and invites you to their "VIP" investing platform. What should you do?
options: Join, since the screenshots prove it works
Invest a small amount to test it
Ask the group members if it's real
Leave the group. Screenshots are easy to fake and this is a common scam
explanation: Many members in these groups are fake accounts. The platform is controlled by scammers, and deposits disappear.
